title: Anabaptists
hook: Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites: adult baptism, simplicity and nonviolence, at great cost

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Anglicans: Cranmer's prayer book and the collect. Your line was a middle way. Where did you find ground that both sides could stand on? Day two hundred ninety-two.

The Netherlands, winter, 1569. A man named Dirk Willems has escaped from prison, where he's been held for his faith, and he's running across a frozen pond. A guard is chasing him. Dirk makes it across; the ice holds his thin, starved body. Behind him, the guard crashes through the ice and starts to drown, screaming for help. Dirk is free. Nobody would blame him for running. He stops. He turns around. He goes back across the ice and pulls his pursuer out of the water. The guard wants to let him go, the story says, but the magistrate on the shore orders him taken. Dirk is led back to prison, and soon after he's burned at the stake. His story is kept in a thick old book of martyrs, the Martyrs Mirror, still found in Amish and Mennonite homes. Today's word is his people.
screen: `A FROZEN POND, 1569.` → `HE TURNS BACK.` → `HE SAVES THE MAN CHASING HIM.`

segments.voice: Anabaptists means rebaptizers, from the Greek ana, again. It was a name their enemies gave them. They said they weren't baptizing anyone again: the baptism of a baby, before it could believe, simply wasn't baptism in their eyes. It began in Zurich, in January 1525, when a small group met in a house, and one of them, Conrad Grebel, baptized a former priest, George Blaurock, as an adult who had chosen to follow Christ. It was dangerous. Catholic and Protestant authorities alike treated infant baptism as the glue of society. Within two years, one of that little group, Felix Manz, was drowned in Zurich's river. Many more Anabaptists were executed in the decades that followed. Out of this came families that still live today. The Mennonites, named for Menno Simons, a Dutch former priest. The Amish, who split from the Mennonites in the 1690s under Jakob Ammann. The Hutterites, who share all their property in common. They differ from each other, but they share a few things. Baptism for believers who choose it. A church separate from the state. Simplicity. And nonviolence, taken straight from the Sermon on the Mount: "resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." Many refuse military service, even at great cost. It's why the Amish choose carefully which technology to let in: not because machines are evil, but to protect the life of the community. And it's why a man running for his life turned back on the ice.
screen: `REBAPTIZERS: A NAME FROM ENEMIES.` · `ZURICH, 1525: A CHOSEN BAPTISM.` · `MENNONITES, AMISH, HUTTERITES.` · `SIMPLICITY AND NONVIOLENCE.` · then, large: `TURN TO HIM THE OTHER ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one simple hour. Settle, and breathe. Pick an hour later today, or tomorrow. No screen in it. No buying anything. Maybe a walk, a meal cooked slowly, a conversation, work with your hands. Picture it now, clearly, what you'll do and where. Notice how much quieter it already feels. If you pray, you can offer that hour to God. If you don't, just let it be an hour of peace, for you and anyone near you. The bell holds the time.
Anabaptists. The rebaptizers, a name from their enemies: Mennonites, Amish and Hutterites, who baptize believers and choose simplicity and peace.
Your line: the peaceable way. Today, live simply for one hour, and when someone crosses you, turn back toward them instead of away. Day two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Anabaptist churches baptize those old enough to choose faith, many refuse military service, and communities such as the Amish and Hutterites live simply, share work, and decide together which modern tools to use.

original.note: Greek: to dip or immerse. With ana, again, it gave the name rebaptizers.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Amish just don't like modern life.
what it means: part of a family of churches born in 1525 that baptizes believers, keeps church and state apart, and chooses simplicity and nonviolence.
what a scholar hears: ana-baptism, an insult. Manz was the first to be executed by a Protestant city, and Martyrs Mirror still keeps the stories.

notes: Editor review (282-299 pass): SERIOUS fix: the trapdoor called Felix Manz 'the first martyr'; Anabaptists had already been executed by Catholic authorities (e.g. Eberli Bolt, Schwyz, 1525), so Manz is now the first executed by a Protestant city. 'Holland' made 'the Netherlands' (Asperen); 'thousands executed' and 'almost every church and government' softened; Martyrs Mirror named and 'many families still own' softened.
Dirk Willems: Asperen, 1569, recorded in Martyrs Mirror (1660). The detail that the guard wanted to release him and the burgomaster insisted comes from the Martyrs Mirror account. Confirm.
First adult baptism: January 21, 1525, in the house of Felix Manz's mother; Grebel baptized Blaurock. Manz drowned January 5, 1527.
Amish division under Jakob Ammann, 1693. Hutterites named for Jakob Hutter (d. 1536).
Not all Anabaptist groups refuse all military service today; script says 'many'.
Greek βαπτίζω note: 'Anabaptist' from Greek ana + baptizo via Latin. Confirm.
